doc.title: George Russell — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Hearing Garbarek and Rypdal and losing them to ECM
summary: He heard Jan Garbarek and Terje Rypdal at a Norwegian festival, formed a group with them, and lost them to Manfred Eicher's ECM.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: As I said, I had gotten a small group of young musicians together between Stockholm and Norway. But before that, I should say, at one of the Norwegian festivals I heard some musicians who never had been out of Norway play, sort of late-night play. I could have been on 125th Street in New York. That’s the way they played.
Is that right? Okay. They had the real jazz feeling, the urban.
Yeah. They were incredible. It was Jan Garbarek . . .
Okay. I was going to ask you about him.
Rypdal. Is that his name? How do you pronounce his last name?
Yeah, but then the drummer was beautiful. I can’t think of his name right now.
We’ll remember his name in a minute.
But you heard them playing, and they had the feeling.

Yeah. I got them all. They all became members of my group. Not – they didn’t just stay in Norway. They moved to Stockholm and did things in Stockholm. When I’d go to Italy or something, they’d go. Finally, they were signed over to a company that only specialized in jazz.
ECM Records. Manfred Eichner or something.

Yeah. Manfred Eicher. That’s right. I felt robbed, because he took all the people. He had heard my group. He made an offer that to me, it didn’t make any sense. But that group became world travelers for a number of years.
